Although coined in the 1960s, “science diplomacy” emerged in the early 21st century among US and UK-based practitioners who promoted science diplomacy as a state-centric, heuristic tool, arguing that it could transform IR. Since science was claimed to be a global, non-ideological endeavor, it could act as a bridge-builder to forge, stabilize, and improve IR, and thus support coalition building and conflict resolution. It could therefore improve bilateral relations and support multilateral efforts addressing common issues, like climate change. Furthermore, international scientific collaboration not only produced beneficial knowledge but also positive, nonscientific externalities, such as cross-cultural understanding and mutual trust. These arguments have largely defined the public discourse on science diplomacy, yet they have also been criticized for being idealistic.
